newsitem.title: CANADA: Trade growth slows among Canadian provinces.
newsitem.headline: Trade growth slows among Canadian provinces.

text.p: Canadian industry found it harder to trade between the country's provinces in the period 1990 to 1995, and dramatically turned to foreign markets, Statistics Canada said on Tuesday.
Trade among the 10 Canadian provinces and two northern territories rose only 6.6 percent, to $150 billion, in the five-year period.
That was due entirely to a 21 percent increase in services, while there was a 3 percent drop in goods.
Industry shifted increasingly heavily to trade on foreign markets, and Canada's exports for 1995 were up 69 percent above their 1990 level, Statistics Canada said.
The shift from inter-provincial trade to foreign markets was most pronounced in Quebec, the mainly French speaking province where separatist influence is strong.

Quebec's interprovincial trade fell to annual deficits of more than $1 billion in 1994 and 1995, following surpluses of about $2 billion earlier in the decade, the federal agency said. Meanwhile, foreign exports rose 78 percent between 1990 and 1995.

Alberta was another province that showed slower growth in interprovincial trade and its trade imbalance with other provinces grew over the period. The province's inter-provincial trade deficit was "more than offset by a foreign trade surplus that reached $10.6 billion in 1995," Statistics Canada said.
